stemOverrides.86: Let \(A(\sec\theta,\ 2\tan\theta)\) and \(B(\sec\phi,\ 2\tan\phi)\), where \(\theta+\phi=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\), be two points on the hyperbola \(2x^{2}-y^{2}=2\). If \((\alpha,\beta)\) is the point of intersection of the normals to the hyperbola at \(A\) and \(B\), then \((2\beta)^{2}\) is equal to ____.

authoredSolutions.75: For \(x\in\left(\frac{\pi}{2},\pi\right)\) we have \(\frac{x}{2}\in\left(\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\), so \(\sqrt{1+\sin x}=\cos\frac{x}{2}+\sin\frac{x}{2}\) and \(\sqrt{1-\sin x}=\sin\frac{x}{2}-\cos\frac{x}{2}\). The argument reduces to \(\frac{2\sin\frac{x}{2}}{2\cos\frac{x}{2}}=\tan\frac{x}{2}=\cot\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{x}{2}\right)\), so \(y=\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{x}{2}\) and \(\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{1}{2}\) throughout the interval, in particular at \(x=\frac{5\pi}{6}\). Hence (A).
authoredSolutions.76: The point with ordinate \(3\) is \((2,3)\). Differentiating \((y-2)^{2}=x-1\) gives \(2(y-2)y'=1\), so the slope at \((2,3)\) is \(\frac{1}{2}\) and the tangent is \(x=2y-4\). Integrating with respect to \(y\) from \(0\) to \(3\), the area enclosed by the parabola \(x=(y-2)^{2}+1\), this tangent and the \(x\)-axis is \(9\) square units. Hence (A).
authoredSolutions.86:
Differentiate the hyperbola \(2x^{2}-y^{2}=2\) implicitly: \(4x-2y\,y'=0\), so the tangent slope at \((x_1,y_1)\) is \(y'=\dfrac{2x_1}{y_1}\) and the normal slope is \(-\dfrac{y_1}{2x_1}\).

At \(A(\sec\theta,\ 2\tan\theta)\) the normal slope is \(-\dfrac{2\tan\theta}{2\sec\theta}=-\sin\theta\). Its equation is
\[y-2\tan\theta=-\sin\theta\,(x-\sec\theta)\ \Rightarrow\ y=-x\sin\theta+\tan\theta+2\tan\theta=-x\sin\theta+3\tan\theta,\]
using \(\sin\theta\sec\theta=\tan\theta\).

Since \(\phi=\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\), we have \(\sec\phi=\csc\theta\) and \(\tan\phi=\cot\theta\). At \(B(\csc\theta,\ 2\cot\theta)\) the normal slope is \(-\cos\theta\), giving
\[y=-x\cos\theta+\cot\theta+2\cot\theta=-x\cos\theta+3\cot\theta.\]

Set the two normals equal to find the intersection:
\[-x\sin\theta+3\tan\theta=-x\cos\theta+3\cot\theta\ \Rightarrow\ x(\cos\theta-\sin\theta)=3(\cot\theta-\tan\theta)=\frac{3(\cos\theta-\sin\theta)(\cos\theta+\sin\theta)}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}.\]
Hence \(\alpha=x=\dfrac{3(\cos\theta+\sin\theta)}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}\).

Now
\[\beta=-\alpha\sin\theta+3\tan\theta=-\frac{3(\cos\theta+\sin\theta)}{\cos\theta}+\frac{3\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}=\frac{-3\cos\theta-3\sin\theta+3\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}=-3.\]

Therefore \((2\beta)^{2}=(-6)^{2}=36.\)
authoredSolutions.90: Write \(2e^{x}+3e^{-x}=A(4e^{x}+7e^{-x})+B(4e^{x}-7e^{-x})\). Matching coefficients gives \(4A+4B=2\) and \(7A-7B=3\), so \(A=\frac{13}{28},\ B=\frac{1}{28}\). The integral becomes \(Ax+B\log_{e}(4e^{x}+7e^{-x})+C=\frac{1}{14}\left(\frac{13}{2}x+\frac12\log_{e}(4e^{x}+7e^{-x})\right)+C\), so \(u=\frac{13}{2},\ v=\frac12\) and \(u+v=7\).
